articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 8: BIR details Duterte's income, confirms tax audit
articles.summary: A Bureau of Internal Revenue official told the impeachment court on Thursday, October 8, that Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband earned a combined P85.34 million in income net of tax from…

blocks.text: October 9, 2026 | 10:32am

MANILA, Philippines — A Bureau of Internal Revenue official told the impeachment court on Thursday, October 8, that Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband earned a combined P85.34 million in income net of tax from 2007 to 2025, and confirmed the bureau has issued a letter of authority to audit one of them.
Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez, chief of staff at the BIR Office of the Commissioner, testified on Article II of the complaint, which accuses Duterte of accumulating unexplained wealth.

She took the stand only in the afternoon after the defense objected to a prosecution request to present forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera first because private prosecutor Erwin Matib, who was handling her direct examination, was ill. Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero instead called an early lunch on Sen. Tito Sotto’s motion.
Over defense objections, Escudero ruled the BIR records are public documents that cannot be prevented from being shown on screen.
Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer, citing the Data Privacy Act, asked that the tax returns not be shown publicly, a concern Sen. Pia Cayetano shared.
The court allowed the BIR’s summaries to be displayed but barred the source documents.
Here are the three highlights from Thursday’s proceedings.
1. Income compared with declared net worth

Matib pointed to a gap between Duterte and Manases Carpio's combined income of P85.34 million and the P98.66 million net worth Duterte declared in her 2025 statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN).
Escudero sided with Ferrer, who objected that the witness had no personal knowledge of the SALN, but did not strike the remark, reminding Matib not to “testify for the witness.”

The couple’s audited financial statements showed cash on hand and in banks rising from P21.23 million at the end of 2022 to P28.97 million in 2023, then falling to P15.53 million in 2024 and P13.80 million in 2025.

Marquez said Duterte signed the attached statement of management’s responsibility as proprietor, meaning she “acknowledges that she is responsible for all the information and representations contained in the annual income tax return” for 2025.
2. Law practice and Davao City salary

Marquez said Duterte is registered with the BIR as a professional in “legal activities.” The financial statements do not state the source of the couple’s “other income,” P1.58 million in 2024 and P1.1 million in 2025, but she said the BIR treats it as income from law practice.
A BIR Form 2316 attached to Duterte’s 2023 return showed she received compensation from the Davao City government that year, her second as vice president.
In showing this, the prosecution cited the constitutional ban on the vice president holding other offices or practicing other professions.

Matib also presented returns from Duterte’s years as Davao City mayor showing non-compensation income of up to P4.65 million a year, despite a Local Government Code ban on mayors practicing their profession. He said this showed “a habit of violating laws which prohibit her from practicing her profession.”

Questioned by Escudero, Marquez confirmed the BIR had issued a letter of authority to audit either Duterte or her husband but declined to give details. “Confidential po ito so I cannot disclose it in this court,” she said.
3. No tax record of Cale88 share transfer

Marquez said the BIR has no record of any transfer of Carpio’s shares in Cale 88 Foods Corp., a Davao banana chips exporter, or of taxes paid on one. No electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (eCAR), required before a sale of unlisted shares can be recorded in a company’s books, has been issued or applied for.
The prosecution argued that Carpio therefore remains the owner and that the sale of his shares to Pikimong Pikimong Inc. was “fake,” a description Escudero struck at the defense’s request.

Matib noted the transfer nonetheless appeared in the company’s General Information Sheet with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Marquez told Escudero the sale remained valid between the parties but “should not have been recorded in the stock and transfer books.”

On cross-examination, Ferrer established that staff of Revenue District Office 113A in Davao City, not the BIR central office, encoded the figures relating to the Dutertes' tax filings, and that Marquez’s office “only reviewed the tax summaries.”

Cross-examination continues on Friday, with Escudero aiming to conclude the testimony of Marquez before lunch so the court can proceed to Cabrera, whose testimony he described as the “meat” of Article II.

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Riyadh airport as airlines suspend flights to Saudi capital
articles.summary:
Saudi Arabia has not commented on claims, but confirmed three killed in airport strikes earlier this week

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis say they have struck Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh ⁠airport…

blocks.text: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis say they have struck Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh ⁠airport with a ballistic missile, badly damaging a plane and leading some airlines to suspend flights to the capital.
The group provided no evidence, and Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the claim.

However, three people briefed on the matter told Reuters that shrapnel from ​an interception or another projectile left a Saudia Airlines commercial plane heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at a terminal on Thursday.
They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the ⁠time but they could not rule out any injuries.

Witnesses heard explosions in Riyadh, including a large blast at the King Khalid international airport. One witness told the Associated Press that fire and ambulance crews were deployed. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from the airport in a video verified by Reuters.
The witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that outgoing flights were halted, and that passengers were instructed to evacuate the airport.

Lufthansa and Air India confirmed they were ⁠suspending flights to Riyadh. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from the airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT on Thursday, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports.
It comes after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the country’s southwest.

The Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and warning workers to stay away from ⁠energy plants, which would be targeted.
Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in ​Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to ‌take back territory from the Houthis.
The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the country’s south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz.

Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden.
Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.

articles.title: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers say
articles.summary: Pike's lawyers say her recovery is "remarkable" as they give an update on her condition after she survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

blocks.text: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers say
Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospital
Christa Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.

In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said.
"Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.
The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

blocks.caption: A mug shot of death row inmate Christa Pike, held at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution (RMSI) in Tennessee and convicted of murdering a schoolmate three decades ago is shown in this 2023 Tennessee Department of Correction booking photograph.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said.
Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.
They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".
Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.
Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.
Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.
Killing Death Row
Could the US death penalty ever die out? A surreal story about a man in Acton, London, who supplied the USA with lethal drugs tips Livvy Haydock into the macabre world of Death Row.

articles.title: QC court postpones Sara Duterte’s grave threats arraignment anew
articles.summary: The arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte on three counts of grave threats was postponed for the second time on Friday, October 9.

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court for the arraignment of her grave threats case on Oct. 9, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — The arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte on three counts of grave threats was postponed for the second time on Friday, October 9.
Duterte appeared before Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, where her arraignment was scheduled for 8:30 a.m.
The arraignment was initially scheduled for September 11 before being moved to October 9.
Duterte’s camp filed a motion for partial reconsideration and a petition for certiorari on Friday. The reason for the latest postponement was not immediately clear from the available reports.
A motion for partial reconsideration asks a court to review part of an earlier ruling, while a petition for certiorari seeks to challenge a court action allegedly made with grave abuse of discretion.

Duterte’s lawyers have previously questioned the trial court’s jurisdiction over the case, arguing that the Constitution grants impeachable officials limited procedural immunity while in office. The court had earlier rejected her bid to dismiss the charges on jurisdictional grounds.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) filed the three counts of grave threats against Duterte on August 11 over remarks she made during an online press conference in November 2024.

During the briefing, Duterte said she had spoken to someone about killing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then House Speaker Martin Romualdez if anything happened to her.
The charges were filed under Republic Act 10175, or the Cybercrime Prevention Act. Duterte has denied the allegations.
The Quezon City RTC issued an arrest warrant against Duterte on September 4 after finding probable cause to hold her for trial. The court set bail at P120,000 for each count.
Duterte posted bail on September 5, paying a total of P360,000 for the three charges.
The alleged threats against Marcos also form part of one of the Articles of Impeachment against Duterte, who faces an impeachment trial before the Senate.

articles.title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ party accuses government of mass detention of members ahead of weekend protest
articles.summary:
Thousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracy

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as…

blocks.text: India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.

Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of ⁠voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.

A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities ⁠didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.

The CJP said that ‌among those detained was a group ‌of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being ‌taken away in a bus to an unknown location.

The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.

blocks.caption: Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi is detained by police, during a protest organised by opposition parties demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi on 7 October 2026.  Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters

blocks.text: The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.

The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the ​resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.

“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who ⁠actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture ​student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over ​police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.

On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of ​using “brute force” to briefly detain ‌party leader Rahul Gandhi, his ​sister Priyanka Vadra, and other ​lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.

BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

articles.title: Author tells B.C. defamation trial sexual assault claim derailed career, ability to write
articles.summary: Author and former UBC creative writing professor Steven Galloway wept as he testified that he can no longer write since unproven allegations of sexual assault derailed his career.

image.caption: Author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway, back, is seen through a window as he leaves B.C. Supreme Court on Tuesday. He told the court on Thursday, amid his defamation trial, that sexual assault claims had derailed him of his ability to write. (THE CANADIAN PRESS/Da

blocks.text: British Columbia
Author and former UBC creative writing professor Steven Galloway wept as he testified that he can no longer write since unproven allegations of sexual assault derailed his career.
'I just can’t do it anymore. I wish I could,' Steven Galloway told a Vancouver courtroom on Thursday
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 08, 2026 9:41 PM EDT | Last Updated: 4 minutes ago

Author and former University of British Columbia (UBC) creative writing professor Steven Galloway wept as he testified that he can no longer write since unproven allegations of sexual assault derailed his career.
"I just can’t do it anymore. I wish I could," he said.
Galloway told the B.C. Supreme Court judge that writing was the "greatest part" of his life.
The defamation lawsuit was launched by Galloway after a former student, known only as A.B., alleged he sexually assaulted her, while others spread the claim on social media.

items: Sexual assault claims 'flat out never happened,' ex-UBC professor tells defamation trial

blocks.text: After Justice Neena Sharma allowed for a short break in testimony on Thursday, Galloway stood and briefly rested his head on a concrete wall behind the witness box.

The court heard he’d been writing a comedy novel to be part of a three-book deal with a major publisher, and a paperback version of his novel The Confabulist was in the works before the allegations surfaced in November 2015.

He said his income from book royalties has "cratered" to about $5,000 to $10,000 a year "tops," and he hasn’t received any invitations for speaking engagements since the woman, with whom he had an affair, accused him of rape and sexual and physical assault.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins
Galloway denied the allegations during his testimony on Wednesday.
On Thursday, his lawyer questioned him about the state of his career.
"I, like every writer, got plenty of bad reviews, and it ruins your lunch, but not your supper," he said.
"I've never had my humanity torn apart the way this process has done that."

items: Former UBC professor tells defamation trial he was 'shocked' by sexual assault accusation

blocks.text: Galloway testified earlier Thursday that people who signed a letter criticizing the university’s handling of the misconduct case against him were subjected to "extremely hurtful" comments, and suffered socially and professionally.

The letter, known as "UBC Accountable," was published in November 2016 with signatories from the literary community including Margaret Atwood, but Galloway said many removed their names after a wave of vitriolic criticism online.
He said people lost jobs and friendships were ruined, and one signatory called him in tears, saying her daughter was never going to speak to her again.
A number of friends, even those who believed in his innocence, would not talk to him anymore because being associated with him would be "career suicide," he said.
Writer Steven Galloway is pictured in his former office at the University of British Columbia in March 2014. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Galloway told the court that "UBC Accountable" became a hashtag that spread widely online, and became an "all-encompassing" term referring to him, and that he reacted with disgust, dismay and horror to the thousands of vitriolic tweets that were published.
He told the court that a reporter from The Canadian Press had phoned him "relentlessly" and came to his home and left messages in his mailbox, seemingly having access to confidential information.

items: B.C. writer Steven Galloway's defamation case clears court hurdle

blocks.text: Galloway said he had attended a hospitality suite during a writer’s festival in October 2016, against his "better judgment," and said some people spoke to him and others saw him and walked out.
He said an article in The Walrus magazine reported that he was given a "standing ovation" at the festival, which he said didn’t happen, and he contacted the publication’s editor about the inaccuracy.
Galloway said the article portrayed the Canadian literature scene as "a den of rapists and rape apologists" who applauded him after his public shaming and firing.
"I still don't quite understand how the editors at The Walrus didn't fact check that," he said.
Galloway said that journalists had been hounding him for interviews ever since the allegations against him were made public. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
He said after he’d won an arbitration award from UBC, he "briefly had the hope" the storm of tweets would subside, but they continued.
Galloway did not get his job back as part of the arbitration.
"I wouldn't have gone back, for a million dollars a year, to that place," Galloway said.
'It doesn't matter what you do'
He said journalists had been pursuing him for interviews "since day one," and he decided to grant one to Globe and Mail columnist Gary Mason, thinking it may cause people to leave him alone.
"The Gary Mason article didn't do anything. If anything, it made it worse," he said. "One thing I've learned through all this is that when a mob starts coming for you, it doesn't matter what you do."

He said he learned about an art show being held in New York in 2018 through defendant Mandi Gray’s Twitter, a "rape narrative" exhibition that didn’t mention him by name, but included the "UBC Accountable" hashtag.

items: Defendant apologizes to B.C. writer days before defamation trial to start

blocks.text: The lawyer for the woman who accused Galloway said Wednesday that his client's defence no longer includes an assertion that Galloway sexually assaulted her, but only that she reported the assaults.
The court heard he got a job cleaning and fixing swimming pools, writing online marketing advertisements, and he currently works as a "boat broker."

articles.title: Everyone loves Anne Carson — even if it took some time for Canada to get her
articles.summary: Anne Carson, the 76-year-old Canadian writer and artist who won the Nobel Prize for literature Thursday, has always been unapologetically — and quietly — herself, friends and admirers say. Sometimes,…

image.caption: Anne Carson, winner of the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2026, sits outside her home at Aegissioa in Reykjavik, Iceland, Oct. 26, 2023. (Kjartan Thorbjoernsson/Golli/Reuters)

blocks.text: Anne Carson, the 76-year-old Canadian writer and artist who won the Nobel Prize for literature Thursday, has always been unapologetically — and quietly — herself, friends and admirers say.
Sometimes, that has meant not being fully recognized or understood in her own country.

Carson's work defies genre, hopping from prose to poetry to essay — sometimes within the same piece. It features imagined conversations between ancient classics figures and modern celebrities, poetry about love and loss and musings on people's (and her own) idiosyncracies.
Carson is also a renowned scholar and translator of Ancient Greek, known for her revival of Sappho's fragments, notably in her book If Not Winter.

International awards recognized Carson's talent early on. Her first book, 1984's Canicula di Anna, won the Quarterly Review of Literature's Betty Colladay Award. In 1996, she won the Lannan Literary Award for Poetry.
Two years later, she was awarded a prestigious Guggenheim Fellowship and, in 2000, a MacArthur Fellowship, also known as the "Genius Grant."
But the lack of Canadian recognition didn't appear to bother her.
"I like to live behind the back of following," she told The Globe and Mail in 2000.

"Early in her career, a lot of people didn't get it or want to get it," said Lucille Friesen-King Edwards, who along with her then-husband co-founded The Word, a Montreal bookstore that Carson frequented when she taught at McGill University in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
"She's very much herself. She does what she does."
Canadian Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature
Canada catches up
Canada eventually caught up, awarding Carson the Canadian Griffin Poetry Prize several times, as well as the Quebec Writers' Federation's A.M. Klein Prize for Poetry.
But her work, known for its depth and playfulness with words, punctuation and layout, has attracted both young readers and elder intelligentsia alike — an "if you know, you know" kind of status.

items: Canadian Anne Carson awarded Nobel Prize in Literature
A crash course in Anne Carson: the books that won the Canadian author the Nobel Prize

blocks.text: Friesen-King Edwards's favourite work of Carson's is The Beauty of the Husband, an examination of a failed marriage that won the author the UK.'s T.S. Eliot Prize in 2001.

Adrian King Edwards, left, and Lucille Friesen-King Edwards co-founded The Word bookstore in Montreal, where Anne Carson used to visit when she taught at McGill University. (Submitted by The Word Bookstore)
Her ex-husband and bookstore co-founder, Adrian King Edwards, pointed out that most of Carson's books do not feature a biography of the writer, only a simple sentence: "Anne Carson lives in Canada."
Still, her books, enigmatic as they may be, rarely last a few hours on the shelves before being picked up by customers, he says.
"On the one hand, her work feels a little niche, but on the other hand, so many people connect with it," said the couple's son, Brendan Edwards.
From poetry to paint and theatre
Carson has illustrated several of her book covers herself, namely a vivid black and red volcano on Glass, Irony and God, and a hand-drawn, animal-like figure on the more recent Wrong Norma.

She has also written plays and art performances. Her translation of Antigone, Sophocles's classic fifth-century BCE tragedy, featured Academy Award-winning French actress Juliette Binoche starring in the titular role and Belgium's Ivo van Hove as director.
Will Aitken, a Montreal writer and Carson's close friend, wrote a book about his experience witnessing the making of the play, which had a profound impact on him.

items: Why Will Aitken wrote a book about Anne Carson's adaptation of Antigone

blocks.text: "This had a lot to do with Anne herself, because she translated this ancient classic and did it in vernacular English," Aitken told CBC while on holiday in Sarajevo.
"She knows how to make things immediate. And she knows how to dive into almost anything and find the core, the heart of emotion and expresses that."
Will Aitken is the Montreal-based author of Antigone Undone, a book about his experience witnessing the making of the play. (Gerald L'Ecuyer/University of Regina Press)

Similarly, Carson has imagined scenarios featuring Ancient Greek or Roman poets and characters conversing colloquially with each other or with present-day celebrities, expressing having modern-day concerns and anxieties.
In her work Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, she stages conversations between Helen of Troy, Helen of Sparta, Marilyn Monroe and Norma Jeane Baker, Monroe's birth name.

"She's thought so hard about time, and it's as if she can walk through it," said Victoria Wohl, a classics professor at the University of Toronto, who says Carson has been an inspiration and regularly teaches her translations.
Love, longing, language
Wohl, too, believes Carson may have been underappreciated as a giant of Canadian literature — though she noted that perhaps winning the world's most distinguished literary award could change that.

She said she first encountered Carson's work when she read Eros: The Bittersweet as a graduate student in the 1990s. The book, which explores desire through classical philosophy and literature, is still widely read despite being among the author's more academic works.
"She's very interested in pothos, which is the love of longing and lack," said Wohl. "And these gaps between people, between words, between understandings."
Wohl said Carson's writing was a departure from other classics scholars, and inspired her to write differently in her own career.

Victoria Wohl is a professor of classical studies at the University of Toronto and regularly incorporates Anne Carson's ancient Greek translations in her teaching. (Submitted by the University of Toronto)
In real life, Wohl said, Carson is "ethereal and otherworldly, and you can sense the brilliance and creativity."

Elizabeth Harvey, a professor emeritus at University of Toronto who is writing a book about the writer, added another perspective: Carson can be disarmingly deadpan, she says, putting audiences "in stitches" when she speaks in public.
The poet showed a glimpse of that sense of humour in a response to the Globe and Mail on Thursday, when the newspaper sought her reaction to winning the Nobel.
Carson — who was in Iceland, where she spends much of her time with her husband, Robert Currie — emailed back a one-word reply: "YIKES!!"
Author Anne Carson learned of Nobel win from Iceland
'Polite, but wrong'
Speaking to the Paris Review in 2024, Carson shared some of the inspiration for the title of her book, Wrong Norma.
"When people ask me, 'How are Canadians different from Americans?' I say, 'Canadians have one characteristic: they’re polite, but wrong.' All the time, polite but wrong," she said.

She is the third Canadian to be awarded the Nobel Prize in literature, and her win comes at a time when the country's entertainment offerings are piquing the world's curiosity and broadening its own horizons.
Anne Carson poses at the National Book Critics Circle Awards in New York in March 1999. (Stephen Chernin/Canadian Press)

Prime Minister Mark Carney — who himself has attracted international attention since being sworn in last year — congratulated Carson in a social media post Thursday, applauding her "wit, imagination and a style entirely her own."
Aitken, her close friend, quipped: "Carney and Anne together have raised the Canadian profile immensely."

items: 'Cool to be Canadian': Leaders optimistic their pitch to invest here will pay off

blocks.text: She continues to publish pieces regularly in the New Yorker and the London Review of Books, where she has recently written about living with Parkinson's disease.
"A symptom particularly mortifying to me was that my handwriting disintegrated," Carson wrote.

As for the future, Carson is already working on her next book, according to Harvey. Aitken noted that she is always occupied — at her home, she uses three different desks, he said, often working on several pieces of art and writing simultaneously.

She has also written about swimming, comparing it to seeking beauty. Aitken recalled a vacation the pair took in Cape Cod decades ago, when his friend would wake up at 5 a.m. every morning to swim in the bay and then write until lunchtime.
"She's constantly overflowing with ideas and concepts and metaphors, and, you know, needs to express them and needs to get them out there."

articles.title: ICC rules Rodrigo Duterte fit to stand trial
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court has ruled that former president Rodrigo Duterte is fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity of murder, saying that he can understand the proceedings and…

blocks.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, for the first time as proceedings over his administration’s “war on drugs” move forward.
International Criminal Court

MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) has ruled that former president Rodrigo Duterte is fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity of murder, saying that he can understand the proceedings and effectively exercise his fair trial rights despite concerns over his health.

In a public redacted decision released on October 8, ICC Trial Chamber III rejected the defense's requests for additional medical examinations and to question the panel of experts who assessed Duterte's fitness to stand trial.
"THE CHAMBER IS SATISFIED that the Accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings and is therefore fit to stand trial," the decision read.

The chamber based its ruling on reports submitted by a panel of three medical experts who examined Duterte. The experts submitted their joint and individual reports on August 21 after being appointed by the chamber in June.

The panel unanimously found that Duterte could understand the charges against him, the purpose and consequences of the proceedings, the evidence and the nature and implications of entering a plea. It also found that he could instruct his lawyers in preparing and conducting his defense.

Duterte's defense team had argued that he “suffers from significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing memories.” It sought further medical examinations and an opportunity to question the experts about their findings.
The chamber denied the requests, noting that the defense had not presented evidence to challenge the medical panel's conclusions.
“The Chamber notes that the Defence has not provided any evidence which contradicts or undermines the findings made by the experts,” the decision read.

The experts found that Duterte remained physically frail and needed medical and nursing care. However, they found no evidence of a worsening mental state or cognitive abilities that would prevent him from standing trial.

The chamber ordered measures to support Duterte during the proceedings, including the use of over-ear headphones or hearing aids, assistance with his food, rest and exercise needs, and access to nursing staff during breaks for medication and care.

It also directed the ICC Registry to continuously monitor Duterte's health and immediately report any changes in his condition. The parties may seek a reassessment of his fitness to stand trial if his health changes.

The chamber said sitting hours would be determined on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the circumstances of the proceedings and the needs of witnesses, including those from the Philippines who will testify through video link.
Duterte's defense team is due to file its pre-trial brief on October 30, a month before the scheduled start of his trial.
Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity over alleged murders linked to his anti-drug campaign from 2013 to 2018, when he was Davao City mayor and president.
Prosecutors allege his involvement in at least 76 murders during the campaign, which resulted in thousands of deaths.

The 81-year-old former president appeared in person before the ICC on September 16 during a status conference. Trial Chamber III later ordered him to remain detained, citing the likelihood that he could abscond or obstruct or endanger the investigation or court proceedings.
His trial is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30, 2026.

articles.title: Michigan Senate hopeful Mike Rogers faces pressure over Trump's trade war
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers faced pressure over U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada during a heated debate that could sway voters in a consequential midterm race where…

image.caption: Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate seat up for grabs in Michigan, is seen speaking during a televised debate at a studio in Grand Rapids, Mich., on Thursday. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers faced pressure over U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada during a heated debate that could sway voters in a consequential midterm race where neither candidate ruled out future duties.
Trump's trade war a ballot issue in close race between Rogers and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed

Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers faced pressure over U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada during a heated debate Thursday that could sway voters in a consequential midterm race in which neither candidate ruled out future tariffs.

Trump's escalating tariffs on Canada came up within the first 10 minutes of the debate. Rogers was asked about an advertisement released Wednesday in which he said "Canada is not our enemy," and how he squares that position with longstanding support for the tariffs.
"I would like to see the deal made," Rogers responded. "I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of Commerce, about getting the deal done."

Rogers said Canada imposes tariffs on U.S. goods, without providing details about the levies or addressing the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, which was negotiated during the first Trump administration.

items: Trump administration faces 2 lawsuits for taxpayer-funded ads as midterms draw near
'Canada is not our enemy': Michigan Republican Senate candidate breaks with Trump on trade war

blocks.text: But the Republican candidate said the U.S. tariffs on Canada are now too high and those should be eliminated.

"This is about getting to the best deal possible. I'd like to it end. I think we need to end it," Rogers said before taking jabs at his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, claiming El-Sayed's policies would raise prices.
The trade war with Canada has become a campaign issue in the close race between Rogers and El-Sayed ahead of the November midterm elections.
Escalating trade war
Trump rapidly escalated his trade war and rhetoric against Canada after negotiations fell apart in August.
Trump reacts to anti-trade war ad from Republican candidate

Trump signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and the United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods. A few weeks later, Ottawa responded with retaliatory duties.
Last week, a U.S. import ban on some Canadian liquor, whey products and motorcycles officially took effect.

Rogers had also previously inserted himself into the dispute over the controversial delay of the Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor and Detroit, claiming "Amer­ica will get a better fin­an­cial deal and that there will be no Chinese cars pour­ing over that bridge."

Polling has shown that a majority of Michigan voters disapprove of Trump's tariffs and his targeting of Canada. Michigan's economy is deeply integrated with Canada's, particularly in the auto industry.
That has put Rogers in a difficult position. He is among a growing number of Republicans distancing their campaigns from some of the president's policies.
Clashes over Iran war, cost of fuel

Thursday's fiery debate also featured clashes over the Iran war, cost of gas and diesel and properties owned by the candidates. Rogers argued El-Sayed's policies would be costly, while the Democrat sought to tie Rogers to Trump's controversial policies, as well as properties outside Michigan and campaign donations.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrats' nominee for the U.S. Senate in Michigan in 2026, is seen participating in a televised debate against Rogers (unseen in the image above) in Grand Rapids, Mich., on Thursday. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)
Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to win a Senate majority, making the Michigan race particularly consequential.
But El-Sayed's response on tariffs is unlikely to reassure Canadians shaken by Trump's trade polices. He was asked about a statement on his website supporting tariffs as long as they are targeted.
While El-Sayed said the tariffs on Canada are costing Michiganders thousands of dollars, he said he supports duties as part of an "industrial policy that makes sense."
"We use tariffs to protect our own market," El-Sayed said.
"This is, like everything, ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving, that Donald Trump does."

articles.title: Counting under way in Holborn and St Pancras byelection – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Results are expected from 2.30am BST in the north London poll to choose a replacement for former PM Keir Starmer

A quick reminder of

blocks.text: Counting under way in Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.
Counting is currently under way in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in north London, where voters are choosing a replacement for former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
Starmer announced his decision to step down as an MP in September after being ousted from No 10 by Andy Burnham.
Camden council has said the result is expected to be called between 2:30-4am UK time.
We’ll bring you the latest developments as we get them.

blocks.caption: Ballots being counted after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in London on Thursday.  Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images

blocks.text: Key events

items: 12m agoWho are the candidates?
18m agoCounting under way in Holborn and St Pancras byelection

blocks.text: Zack Polanski’s had a tricky week leading up to the byelection amid criticism he showed a lack of leadership over a policy equating Zionism with racism adopted at last weekend’s Green party conference
Polanski missed the vote on it in Brighton in order to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

But the Greens’ adoption of the policy has been highly contentious – drawing sharp rebukes from mainstream UK parties, British Jewish groups and Israel – while also prompting four of five Green MPs to publicly reject the move.

The motion said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism” and called for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. The head of the Jewish Greens condemned it and said she might leave the party, although it was supported by some Jewish Greens.

Even members who supported large parts of the motion were unhappy about its narrow conception of Zionism which some fear could brand those in favour of the idea of a Jewish homeland – but not specifically the modern-day state of Israel – as racist.
The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after their adoption of the policy drew dismay from the group representing European Greens.
Who are the candidates?
A quick reminder of the byelection candidates in Holborn and St Pancras:

items: Labour – Sagal Abdi-Wali
Green party – Zack Polanski
Conservative party – Ewan Cameron
Reform UK – Peter Newman
Liberal Democrats – Patrick Thomas Stillman
Restore Britain – Tyler Kurtis Johnson
Workers party – George Galloway
Rejoin EU – Briony Anne Lonbay Kapoor
Climate party – Clare Fischer
UK Voice – Ketankumar Pipaliya
Ukip – Ben Walker
Monster Raving Loony party – Barmy Brunch
Communist League – Jonathan Silberman
Christian Peoples Alliance – Helen Spiby-Vann
Independent – Tom Darwood

blocks.caption: Peter Walker

blocks.text: Peter Walker
Holborn and St Pancras is, under normal circumstances, a Labour stronghold.

Keir Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Zack Polanski. In 2019 Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes.

Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign. He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat.

blocks.caption: Green leader Zack Polanski (second right) campaigning on the streets of Holborn and St Pancras last month. Photograph: Andy Hall/The Guardian

blocks.text: However, the political landscape has changed. Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour.

Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies.

Polanski’s fortunes, in contrast, appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party.

articles.title: Alberta premier unclear when asked to define threshold for questions 1 to 9 on referendum ballot
articles.summary: On Thursday, CBC News asked Premier Danielle Smith to define what she considers a strong mandate and what the thresholds will be for taking action on each question.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks at a news conference in Edmonton on Oct. 8, 2026. (Scott Neufeld/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton
On Thursday, CBC News asked Premier Danielle Smith to define what she considers a strong mandate and what the thresholds will be for taking action on each question.
Albertans can vote on 9 questions about immigration and constitutional issues on Oct. 19

Premier Danielle Smith was not clear on Thursday when asked what she considers a strong mandate to move forward on policies about immigration and constitutional issues after Albertans vote in this month’s provincial referendum.

On Oct. 19, Albertans can vote on five questions about immigration and four questions relating to Canada’s Constitution, along with a question added by the provincial government about separatism: whether to stay in Canada or hold a second binding referendum on separating from the country.

While Smith has said she considers 50 per cent plus one a threshold for the question about separatism, she demurred when asked by CBC News at an unrelated news conference on Thursday what she considers a strong mandate or a threshold for the other nine questions.
“I’m going to look at what the results are," she said. "We are very pleased that there’s a lot of interest in participating in this vote.

"We want to make sure that there’s a lot of feedback from Albertans. So we’ll look at the voter turnout and we’ll look at the results and we’ll be able to give you some clear direction on Oct. 20 once we’ve heard from Albertans."
Paperwork for a special mail-in ballot for Alberta’s 2026 referendum is shown. (Nate Luit/CBC)
Smith was pressed on why Albertans are not being given a clear definition of what the government considers a strong mandate before they cast their ballots.

“I think people know that I want these nine [proposals] to get an endorsement," she said. "I don’t want to prejudge the outcome, but I’ve made it pretty clear that I would like to proceed on these nine issues.
"We heard about it through the Alberta Next Panel, but I want to hear from Albertans to make sure that they agree that this is the right direction to go."

At an announcement on April 23 to unveil a new website for the government's fall referendum questions, Smith said her government wants "voters at the ballot box who have considered the facts carefully, and we want a strong mandate to deliver change for Albertans."
CBC News asked Smith why the province is not using the benchmark of 50 per cent plus one.
“Fifty per cent plus one is normally … what you would use, sure,” she said on Thursday as her press secretary cut off the CBC News reporter who was attempting to clarify her response.

The five questions about immigration relate to whether there should be increased provincial control over immigration, whether non-permanent residents should be prohibited from accessing provincially-funded programs, whether non-permanent residents should be restricted for at least 12 months before qualifying for provincially-funded social support programs, whether non-permanent residents should be charged a fee for health care and education and whether proof of citizenship should be required to vote in provincial elections.

articles.title: Sydney festival 2027: 11 international dance works to headline ‘once-in-a-lifetime’ program
articles.summary: Making its southern hemisphere debut, Dance Reflections will feature collaborators of Rosalía, Madonna and Beyoncé – and a high-wire takeover of the Cutaway

blocks.text: A “once-in-a-lifetime” program of dance works of scale will be coming to Sydney in January, including 11 international works from France, Belgium, South Africa and beyond making their Australian premiere.

The program, which triples the scale of the dance offering at the last Sydney festival, will bring 174 performers and crew to Sydney, with the crowning jewel being the acclaimed French choreographer Rachid Ouramdane’s Outsider. The 2024 work features 21 dancers from the Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève and four elite athletes, navigating a “cat’s cradle” of high wires and slack lines, to the mesmerising, minimalist music of the avant garde composer Julius Eastman.

Outsider will be performed in a purpose-built 720-seat theatre in the recently renovated Cutaway at Barangaroo – the first time the space has been activated for theatrical performance. The venue will also host Christos Papadopoulos’s My Fierce Ignorant Step; a double bill of works by the Chinese choreographer Tao Ye with his company TAO Dance Theatre; and a new work by genre-defying collective (La)Horde, best known for their work with pop stars such as Madonna, Sam Smith and Rosalía.

blocks.caption: Rambert in Hop(e)storm by (La)Horde, who will be bringing a new work to Sydney. Photograph: Hugo Glendinning

blocks.text: Under the banner of the Sydney festival, which announces its full program on 19 October, this is the first southern hemisphere outing for Dance Reflections, an international festival funded by French jewellery maison Van Cleef and Arpels, which has previously been staged in cities such as London, New York, Hong Kong and Seoul.

“Dance Reflections has been a real gamechanger in the creation and dissemination of dance on this scale,” says the Sydney festival director, Kris Nelson, who witnessed first-hand the impact the inaugural festival had in London, where he was working at the time.

In Sydney, he says, it will be a “once-in-a-lifetime” opportunity for dance lovers, including the Australian debuts of Ouramdane, (La)Horde and the rising star Leïla Ka, who has choreographed for Beyoncé. The Belgian master Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker will return to Australia with her company Rosas, and, from Australia, there’s a brand new work from Indigenous and intercultural dance company Marrugeku.

blocks.caption: Marrugeku’s artistic directors Dalisa Pigram and Rachael Swain. The Indigenous and intercultural dance company will be premiering a new work at Dance Reflections. Photograph: Philip Thompson

blocks.text: It’s been more than a decade since Sydney’s last major dance festival, Spring Dance. Launched by the Sydney Opera House in 2009, it ran for four years and featured superstars such as Akram Khan and Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, before being dropped in 2013 for financial reasons. At the time, the Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron described the city’s dance audience as “relatively small but passionate”.

Nelson is hoping that’s changed. “I’m not daunted,” he says, pointing to the viral popularity of dance on TikTok, and the pop cultural work of choreographers such as (La)Horde and Leïla Ka, who draw from queer club culture and street dance.
after newsletter promotion

The festival is offering 10,000 A-Reserve tickets across the program at $49, and two works will be free: Trisha Brown’s seminal Roof Piece, in the gallery spaces of the Art Gallery of NSW; and the Belgian choreographer Cassiel Gaube’s tribute to house music, Soirée d’études, in the public space at Carriageworks.

“I’m really excited because we’re presenting a massive sampler of different kinds of dance, from the super classical to the acrobatic, to clubby and queer, personality-driven dance with big characters on stage, and works where you’re watching these incredible bodies do amazing geometry,” Nelson says. “This is your chance to test it out.”

articles.title: Jim Chalmers overrules ATO’s controversial ban on credit card payments following business outcry
articles.summary:
Treasurer earmarks funds for year-long transition period for tax office, delaying ban’s 30 November start date

  • Get our

blocks.text: A controversial ban on credit card payments on tax bills will be delayed by more than six months, after the federal government overruled the tax office and announced new stopgap funding.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, announced extra funding on Friday, after days of criticism and calls from small business to halt the ban.
The tax office will continue to accept credit card payments via third parties as well as other free and low-fee payment methods like debit card and bank transfers from July 2027.
The decision came after criticism of the ATO’s response to the Reserve Bank’s moves to ban credit card surcharges, something the federal government sought to take credit for.
The tax commissioner, Rob Heferen, announced moves in early October to stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from 1 December.
He said continuing to accept card payments would cost the ATO almost $200m a year, as those costs can no longer be passed on to card users.

But some business owners, particularly smaller operators, use credit card payments as a cashflow tool, managing their liabilities by using credit when required. Estimates suggest about 5% of small businesses use credit card payments for tax bills.
Because tax liabilities are legislated by federal parliament, the ATO said it could not build card payment costs into charges paid by taxpayers.
Government ministers had sought to pressure the ATO into changing its position this week, amid strong criticism from the Coalition and business lobby groups.
The ATO is an independent authority and the government cannot direct the tax commissioner’s decisions.
Chalmers said the extension would give the ATO time to consult small business to get the policy right.

“Now we try not to interfere with the RBA or the ATO when they go about designing and implementing this surcharge ban, but it’s really important that we have stepped in today to make it possible for the ATO to continue to take credit card payments until the end of the financial year,” he said.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, urged the government to scrap the ban on credit cards, rather than delay it.
“Instead of screwing businesses today, they’ve decided they’re going to screw them … at least in nine months’ time,” he told News24.
“The prime minister should scrap this treasurer while he’s at it, because frankly, this is just another humiliating backdown.”
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss, Andrew McKellar, said the delay provides “much needed breathing space for small business”.
“It is reassuring to see some sense prevail on the credit card ban for now,” he said.
“This is a win for small business and a welcome reprieve, but small businesses remain under significant pressure.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte appears in QC court for grave threats arraignment
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte appeared before a Quezon City court on Friday, October 9, for her arraignment on three counts of grave threats.

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court for the arraignment of her grave threats case on Oct. 9, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte appeared before a Quezon City court on Friday for her arraignment on three counts of grave threats.
The proceedings were scheduled for 8:30 a.m. before Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court.

During an arraignment, the charges are formally read to the accused, who is then asked to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty for each count. If Duterte pleads not guilty, the case will proceed to trial.

The court initially scheduled the arraignment for September 11 but deferred it after granting a motion from Duterte’s camp. The court ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to comment on the motion before resolving it.

Duterte’s lawyers have questioned the trial court’s jurisdiction over the case, arguing that the Constitution grants impeachable officials limited procedural immunity while in office. The court had earlier rejected her bid to dismiss the charges on jurisdictional grounds.
The DOJ filed the three counts of grave threats on August 11 over Duterte’s remarks during an online press conference in November 2024.

During the briefing, Duterte said she had spoken to someone about killing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then House Speaker Martin Romualdez if anything happened to her.
The charges were filed under Republic Act 10175, or the Cybercrime Prevention Act. Duterte has denied the allegations.
On September 4, the Quezon City RTC issued an arrest warrant against Duterte after finding probable cause to hold her for trial. The court set bail at P120,000 for each count.
Duterte posted bail on September 5, paying a total of P360,000 for the three charges.
The case will be heard as Duterte faces an impeachment trial before the Senate. The alleged threats against Marcos also form part of one of the Articles of Impeachment against the vice president.

articles.title: U.S. ICE agents shoot and wound man during arrest in New York City
articles.summary: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in New York City while making an arrest, officials say.

image.caption: A car surrounded by police tape at the scene of a shooting Thursday in Manhattan. (Seth Weni/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in New York City while making an arrest, officials say.
Mayor says he will talk to president and demand ICE enforcement ends in his city

U.S. federal immigration agents shot and wounded a Dominican man while arresting him in New York City on Thursday, in what the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) called a "targeted enforcement operation."
Protesters said it was an example of the dangers of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

The man survived and is being treated at a hospital, DHS said. It did not describe exactly what led to the shooting, saying only that an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer "discharged his weapon" during the incident and the man was injured.

The department described the man as a "criminal illegal alien" with a prior grand larceny conviction and a history of other arrests. He was arrested in December 2023 but was released, DHS said, blaming "reckless" policies in Democrat-led cities such as New York.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for an end to all ICE raids in the city in a statement on social media. Demonstrators at the scene chanted, "ICE off our streets now!"
A person holds a sign near the scene of the shooting. (Seth Wenig/The Associated Press)

An FBI spokesperson said an evidence response team was responding to the scene "to support our partners at the Department of Homeland Security," but offered no other details. Messages seeking further information were sent to federal authorities.
The shooting happened in the Marble Hill neighborhood, a small part of Manhattan attached to the Bronx.
Difficult to identify ICE agents, resident says

Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard about three or four gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with DHS branding.
Witnesses, he said, were screaming.
Neighbourhood resident Alfred Silva, 38, called for federal officers to more clearly identify themselves, saying one was wearing a construction safety vest and carrying a rifle.
"We need to have better transparency to understand who we're dealing with, because anybody in the street can just put on a vest and pull out a gun and claim to be ICE," Silva said.
"I feel like regardless if you're left or right, we should understand that this shouldn't be happening."
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, said in a post on social media that she had been briefed on the shooting.
"We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why," she said.

Another video shows New York City police officers picking up an apparently injured man and carrying him into a police vehicle. Nearby, a damaged car blocking the roadway is seen with small holes in two of its windows.

articles.summary: The shooting happened in the afternoon in the Bronx, with details still emerging. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned the incident and urged Donald Trump to end ICE actions in the city.

image.caption: New York leaders are calling for answers and action following the shooting as protests erupt Image: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: A man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent during an arrest, New York City metropolitan police said Thursday.
What do we know so far?
The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. local time (2100 GMT) in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, which is one of New York's five boroughs.
Details are still emerging, but the New York Police Department has denied that its personnel were involved in the shooting.
"The individual who was shot is at a nearby hospital and is currently conscious and receiving medical attention," the NYPD said in a statement.
US President Donald Trump's administration has scaled up ICE raids in major US cities to detain and deport people who are in the US illegally.
Local media in New York said ICE was involved in the latest shooting in the Bronx, which has sparked protests.

blocks.caption: People at the scene of the shooting expressed their dismay with federal immigration raids in New York CityImage: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: Mamdani says he is contacting Trump to end ICE actions in NYC
New York City Zohran Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he is calling President Trump.

"This is an unconscionable and incredible serious situation," Mamdani said in a post on X. "I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agent terrorize our communities.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul earlier said she has been briefed on the incident.
"We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding the incident," Hochul said in a statement posted on X.
"New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why."
The Department of Homeland Security is the parent agency of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). DHS has not yet publicly commented on the incident.
ICE, CBP fatal shootings raise alarm in second Trump term
Deadly ICE and Border Patrol shootings have drawn major controversy during Trump's second term, particularly regarding the training and oversight of the agents.
An ICE agent killed a 37-year-old US citizen, Renee Good, during their operations in Minnepolis in January, triggering demonstrations there and in several other US cities.
Later that month, Alex Pretti, another US citizen, was killed by two US Customs and Border Protection officers agents in Minneapolis following an altercation.

articles.title: B.C. teen rescued from 'Widowmaker' mountain trail says AI isn't to blame
articles.summary: Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday after accidentally taking what's called "the Widowmaker" climbing route.

image.caption: Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday after accidentally taking what's called 'the Widowmaker' climbing route. The Vancouver teen is pictured here on a hike in September 2026. (Joelle Gowryluk)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday after accidentally taking what's called "the Widowmaker" climbing route.
Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday
A B.C. teen making global headlines after being rescued from the side of a mountain says AI is not the reason he became stranded.

Bryce Gowryluk, 16, an experienced hiker from Vancouver, is frustrated by this week's news stories claiming he used Anthropic's AI chatbot, Claude, to plan the alpine scramble that ended in a helicopter extraction from what's called "the Widowmaker" climbing route on Crown Mountain.
"People are really taking it out of context, because people think that I planned … or was coerced by the AI to go on the Widowmaker, which is not true," Gowryluk told CBC News.
"I just feel like people who are judging the situation are really unfair in their stance."

Volunteer rescue organization North Shore Rescue posted on Facebook Sunday that they responded to a call the day before about a hiker stranded on Crown Mountain, at the base of the final, vertical climbing wall of the route known as the Widowmaker.
They eventually located him by helicopter. A rescue tech belayed down to the hiker and moved him to "a suitable extraction point," and they airlifted him out.
The harrowing photos, and a rescuer's comments that the teen used AI to plan his route, quickly went viral.
A photo posted by North Shore Rescue on Sunday shows a teen who had to be rescued from the side of Crown Mountain, north of Vancouver, the day before. (North Shore Rescue/Facebook)

Gowryluk says he spent three days planning what was meant to be about the eight-hour hike Saturday from the top of Grouse Mountain to Crown Mountain and back. He consulted AllTrails and Google Maps, and admits he cross-referenced some information about the terrain using Claude, but says he mostly used the AI agent to help him with his packing list.

He left home around 7:30 a.m., took the bus to Grouse Mountain, rode the gondola to the top and walked to the alpine trailhead. His route was meant to eventually take him through a rugged scramble, but instead he mistakenly turned onto an unmarked route called the "Widowmaker Arete."
"There's no warnings," he said.

At first, he says, the terrain was "nothing too extreme," so he assumed he was on the right path — until it became too steep and too smooth to count as a scramble at all. Going back down, backwards, wasn't an option, and neither was staying still on the rock face, he said.
"That's when I realized something has gone terribly wrong," Gowryluk said, but he kept climbing, focused on putting his hands and feet wherever they would fit.
"I knew that fear would just lead me to panic, and panic would lead me to my death."
He finally made his way to a ledge wide enough to stand on and called his mom.
LISTEN | Rescuer recalls getting to teen stranded on mountain:
As It Happens6:32Rescuer cautions against 'blindly following' AI directions after chatbot leads teen hiker astray
'I think I made a wrong turn'
Joelle Gowryluk says her phone rang in the early afternoon.

Bryce is an air cadet with survivalist training and is a certified belayer, she said, and so Joelle felt her son was well prepared for yet another hike — especially in a busy area like Grouse on a sunny, clear day.
But when she answered the phone and asked what was going on, Bryce said, "I think I made a wrong turn," Joelle said.
"He wasn't frantic. He just said, 'Mom, I have to call the North Shore Rescue. I can't go any further. I've climbed too high and I can't get back down.'"

North Shore Rescue search manager Paul Markey said they were dispatched by the police to rescue Gowryluk, who he described as "an adventurous sort." And regardless of whether it was via chatbot or his own navigation, Markey says Gowryluk found himself on a significantly challenging alpine climbing route without the proper equipment.
"He was perched on a ledge," Markey told CBC Radio's As it Happens.
"He was very scared, as would [be] anybody in that particular position."

They flew to him quickly, Markey said, and hoisted two rescuers down to him from the helicopter. Then they got him to an area where he could safely be hoisted back up, and brought him back down to the base of the mountain.
"It was definitely, a really try-not-to-freak out experience," Gowryluk said, recalling dangling from the helicopter by a harness.
A still image taken from a video provided by Bryce Gowryluk of Vancouver shows the helicopter that rescued him from Crown Mountain on Saturday. (Bryce Gowryluk)
Experts warn about relying on AI
Bryce came home that day "pretty shocked," Joelle Gowryluk recalled. Typically, he returns from the mountains very happy and very tired, she said, "but a good tired."

Climbing is positive for his mental health, she added, saying she'll continue to encourage him to hike and climb safely — and always with another person — and hopes other teens will consider it, too. But she worries about the media attention that she feels has focused on Bryce's use of AI while downplaying his experience.
"He's no stranger to these North Shore mountains," she said.
When CBC asked Bryce Gowryluk when he might head back for another mountain hike, he replied, "probably Saturday."

items: Maritime experts urge use of verified weather reports after kayaker capsizes in B.C. waters
Rescues in the Rockies cost millions each year. Who pays for them?

blocks.text: While the hiker and rescuer give different reports for how AI was involved in Gowryluk's ill-fated trip, it's just one recent example where chatbots were involved in people finding themselves in dangerous situations.
In September, for instance, maritime first responders warned people not to rely on AI for weather reports after rescuing a man whose kayak capsized on B.C.'s south coast.
He had tried to use an AI chatbot to determine the safest time to paddle.

Markey says the North Shore Rescue probably gets about 150 calls per year, but that Gowryluk's was the first call they'd ever had about someone potentially led into a dangerous area by AI. He's worried it will just be the first of many, he added, and cautioned climbers from "blindly following" a route suggested by artificial intelligence.
"Claude has never been onto that mountain," Markey said.
Bryce Gowryluk, now 16, is pictured hiking as a child. Bryce is an experienced hiker, an air cadet with survivalist training and a certified belayer. (Joelle Gowryluk)

articles.title: Ombudsman vows to protect IP rights after suspending Puerto Princesa exec
articles.summary: In a statement on October 7, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla cited the agency's decision finding Carlo Benitez Gomez, Department Head II of the Puerto Princesa City Environment and Natural Resources…

blocks.text: Office of the Ombudsman along Agham Road in Quezon City.
Wikipedia / patrickroque01

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman reaffirmed its commitment to safeguard the rights of indigenous cultural communities against unlawful and improper government operations, following a ruling that penalized a Puerto Princesa City environmental official for bypassing required indigenous clearances in a river dredging project.

In a statement on October 7, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla cited the agency's decision finding Carlo Benitez Gomez, Department Head II of the Puerto Princesa City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO), administratively liable for Conduct Unbecoming of a Public Officer.
Gomez was meted a penalty of one-year suspension without pay.
Should the suspension no longer be enforceable due to separation from service, the penalty will be converted into a fine equivalent to six months of his salary.

The case stemmed from a complaint filed by the leadership of Sambayaang Tagbanua kat Barangay Simpokan Inc. (STBSI), representing part-owners of an ancestral domain belonging to the Tagbanua Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) in Brgy. Simpokan, Puerto Princesa City.
In 2022, local barangay officials passed a resolution for the rehabilitation and dredging of the Malinao River to mitigate flooding following Typhoon Odette.

Serving as technical secretariat of the City Mining Regulatory Board (CMRB), Gomez issued a clearance to proceed with the project, which allowed the rehabilitation contractor to receive 6,000 cubic meters of surplus gravel extracted from the river to offset operational costs.

STBSI strongly opposed the project, citing a lack of proper consultation, the desecration of their ancestral waters, and a direct violation of Section 59 of Republic Act No. 8371, or the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act (IPRA) of 1997.

In its decision, the Ombudsman held that Gomez issued the project clearance prior to obtaining the required Certification Precondition from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) and without waiting for final approval from the CMRB.

“Gomez's act of issuing clearance to proceed without the required certification precondition from the NCIP and without waiting for the CMRB's approval is a deliberate transgression of rules or procedures as provided under the IPRA,” the Ombudsman’s ruling read.

“Gomez failed to observe professionalism and justness and sincerity so as to discourage wrong perception of his role as a dispenser or peddler of undue patronage. Such conduct or behavior is considered unbecoming of a public officer,” it added.

Meanwhile, participating barangay officials — including the former Barangay Captain, seven councilors, and the Sangguniang Kabataan chairman — were cleared of administrative liability, as their involvement was limited to passing a resolution regarding the river's overflow.

Remulla issued a warning to public officials to strictly adhere to laws protecting indigenous rights, emphasizing that the anti-graft watchdog will continue to act against illegal and unjust acts affecting IP communities.
